diagnostic_evidence.quote: However, for a more general case where $A$ is an invertible M-matrix, more efforts are required.
As we can see from Example \ref{L}, for a general vector equation $Ax-\|x\|_1x=b$, Newton iteration and SDA may not apply. We leave this general problem as a future investigation.

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract and introduction claim existence, uniqueness, and algorithms for every invertible M-matrix with nonnegative b. The analysis instead assumes the special representation $A=(2-\|a\|_{\w})I-T_n(a)$ (or its nonnegative-matrix analogue), together with $\|a\|_{\w}<1$ and the smallness condition $\|b\|_1<(1-\|a\|_{\w})^2$. The paper itself states that the general invertible-M-matrix problem remains future work.

failure_location.quote: where $A$ is an invertible $M$-matrix and $b$ is a nonnegative vector. Existence and uniqueness of a nonnegative solution is proved.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the abstract, introduction, title-level description, and scope statements to the special matrix and small-data regime actually analyzed; otherwise a new theory for arbitrary invertible M-matrices is required.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's principal stated scope, including general existence and uniqueness and general applicability of Newton and SDA, is unsupported.
issues.title: Advertised arbitrary invertible M-matrix scope is not established
issues.why_classification: The source supports only withdrawal of the advertised general regime; preserving it would require new global existence, uniqueness, and convergence arguments.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For given $\epsilon>0$, if $\|v_2\|_1<\epsilon$ and  equation \eqref{eq:v2} has a solution $y$ such that $\|g\|_{\w }+\|y\|_1<1$, then  it satisfies $\|v_1-y\|_1<c\epsilon$ for some constant $c$.
Set $c=\frac{3-\|g\|_{\w}}{2-2\|g\|_{\w}-\mu_1-\|y\|_1},$ then $c>0$ and we have $\|v_1-y_1\|_1\leq c\epsilon$.

This provides some insights on the  numerical treatment of the vector $v_G$, that is, if the constant $c$ is small,  we may compute the solution of equation \eqref{eq:v2}, followed by extending the solution to an infinite vector.

issues.failure_explanation: The truncation tail can be made smaller than epsilon, but the resulting constant c depends on the truncation-dependent quantities $\mu_1$ and $\mu_y$. No bound uniform in p or epsilon is proved. Thus $c\epsilon$ is not shown to tend to zero, and the lemma's existence of some c for each fixed epsilon does not establish convergence of the finite nonlinear solutions to $v_G$.

failure_location.quote: In this paper, we show that the vector $v_G$ can be approximated by a vector  $\widehat{v}_G=(v^T,0)^T$,  where $v\in \mathbb R^p$ for sufficiently large $p$, and solves an equation that can be formulized as equation \eqref{eq:nonlinear}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Prove a truncation-independent positive lower bound for $2-2\|g\|_{\w}-\mu_1-\mu_y$, or otherwise supply a stability argument yielding an error constant uniform for all sufficiently large p; alternatively weaken the text to a conditional heuristic.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed approximation of the infinite correction vector by solutions of the finite equation is unsupported as an asymptotic statement.
issues.title: Finite-section approximation lacks a uniform error argument
issues.why_classification: A nontrivial uniform stability argument is needed, but it is localized to the finite-section reduction; alternatively the approximation promise must be materially weakened.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Suppose $x$ is a solution of equation \eqref{eq:equation1}, then we have $x=(A-\mu_xI)^{-1}b$

issues.failure_explanation: A solution of $(A-\|x\|_1I)x=b$ need not make $A-\|x\|_1I$ invertible. For example, take n=1, $a=0$, $A=2$, and $b=0$, which satisfies the stated assumptions. Then $x=2$ solves $2x-|x|x=0$, but $A-|x|I=0$, so the inverse used in the claimed equivalence is undefined.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the lemma to solutions for which $A-\|x\|_1I$ is nonsingular, in particular to $\|x\|_1\leq1-\|a\|_{\w}$, and state the converse only where the inverse exists.
issues.overall_effect: The global equivalence between all vector-equation solutions and fixed points is false, although its restriction to the sought regime $\|x\|_1<1-\|a\|_{\w}$ remains usable.
issues.title: Solution–fixed-point equivalence ignores singular shifts
issues.why_classification: A short local restriction repairs the lemma while preserving every later use involving the small-norm solution.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Moreover,  it satisfies that $T_n(a)\geq 0$,  $\|a\|_{\w}<1$, and $b\in \mathbb R^n$ is a nonnegative vector

issues.failure_explanation: The assumptions allow $b=0$, for which $g(0)=0$, not strictly positive, so the sign-change argument does not produce an interior root. The theorem remains true in this case because the only solution in the required norm range is $x_*=0$, but that separate boundary case is not proved.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Handle $b=0$ separately, taking $x_*=0$ and using invertibility of $A-\mu I$ throughout the target interval to prove uniqueness; retain the existing argument for $b\neq0$.
issues.overall_effect: The stated existence and uniqueness theorem is not proved for one allowed degenerate input.
issues.title: Existence proof omits the permitted zero right-hand side
issues.why_classification: A short boundary-case argument completes the proof without changing the theorem or any rate or algorithm.

issues.failure_explanation: The preceding analysis establishes a 1-norm bound, not $\|u_kv_k^T\|_\infty<1$; neither matrix norm generally bounds the other in the direction required. Thus the stated inference is unsupported. For the nonnegative rank-one matrix, however, the already proved scalar bound $v_k^Tu_k<1$ directly gives $\rho(u_kv_k^T)<1$ and hence a nonnegative inverse.

issues.failure_explanation: The discarded terms include $\Delta A\,\Delta x$ and $(e^T\Delta x)\Delta x$. They are $O(\epsilon^2)$ only after establishing $\Delta x=O(\epsilon)$, which is precisely the conclusion sought. Existence of nearby perturbed solutions alone does not justify that estimate. The norm step also needs $|e^T\Delta x|\leq\|\Delta x\|_1$, not merely the one-sided inequality written.
